list.listitem: No single clinical or radiographic finding or constellation of findings accurately differentiates community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) caused by Chlamydophila pneumoniae (formerly Chlamydia pneumoniae) from any other cause. C
No accurate, rapid, widely available diagnostic test exists to identify C. pneumoniae. B Combination PCR and serology seem most accurate for diagnosis. C

Treatment of undifferentiated CAP should be empiric and dictated by local microbial patterns and antibiotic resistance patterns; specific coverage of C. pneumoniae in patients with undifferentiated CAP does not reduce mortality. B
Treatment of culture or serologically proven C. pneumoniae includes doxycycline or a macrolide as first-line therapy, or a fluoroquinolone as an alternative. B

background.definition: Chlamydia pneumonia is a LRTI caused by the atypical pathogen Chlamydophila pneumoniae (previously: Chlamydia pneumoniae).

list.listitem: Exact incidence is difficult to estimate. The Global Burden of Disease 2021 study estimated that Chlamydia spp. accounts for 5.4% of global lower respiratory tract infections .
New cases, as a percentage of all cases of CAP, range from 0% to 44% and vary by population studied and diagnostic methods used.
Lack of standardized diagnostic methods adds to the difficulty in estimating incidence.

Among trainee soldiers with X-ray-confirmed pneumonia in Missouri from 2013-2014, monthly rates of chlamydia pneumonia peaked at 0.9/100 trainees in May. Results of NAAT testing of 141 ill trainees demonstrated 37% were positive for chlamydia; this was the most common organism identified in this cohort.

Co-infection with chlamydia occurs in patients with COVID-19-associated pneumonia. In one study of 250 hospitalized patients with COVID-19, 39 (15.6%) tested positive for at least one respiratory pathogen. The most commonly detected CAP pathogen was C. pneumoniae (5.2%), followed by the respiratory syncytial virus (4.8%), M. pneumoniae (4.4%) and adenovirus (2.8%). In an Italian study of 721 patients hospitalized with pneumonia, 443 individuals (61.4%) were infected with SARS-CoV-2 and 242 individuals had an antibody positivity against Mycoplasma and/or C. pneumoniae. Patients with co-infection in this study were more likely to have 3 or more co-morbidities and more likely to be critically ill and require mechanical ventilation.
In a retrospective cohort study of 314 ICU-patients ≥18 years with hospital-acquired respiratory tract infections, none tested positive for C. pneumoniae.
C. pneumoniae is a potential cause of pneumonia outbreaks in the nursing home and prison settings.

Seropositivity to chlamydia heat shock protein-60 antibodies, a marker of chronic chlamydial infection, is associated with increased risk for subsequent lung cancer (odds ratio [OR] 1.30, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.02-1.67). A similar increased risk of lung cancer with C. pneumoniae infection was found in a meta-analysis (OR 1.16, 95% CI 1.00-1.36 in prospective studies and OR 2.17, 95% CI 1.79-2.63 in retrospective studies).
There is an association between C. pneumoniae and atherosclerosis (OR 2.25, 95% CI 1.91 to 2.64), based on a meta-analysis of 38 papers.
Authors of a meta-analysis found an association between C. pneumoniae by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and cerebrovascular disease (OR 1.90, 95% CI 1.17-3.07).
There is an association between both C. pneumoniae (OR 6.34. 95% CI 2.83-14.19) and Chlamydophila psittaci (OR 29.05, 95% CI 8.91-94.70) and schizophrenia.
Persistent C. pneumoniae infection also appears to be associated with overweight/obesity.
C. pneumoniae infection is implicated in some cases of reactive arthritis.

C. pneumoniae may also be associated with Alzheimer disease, chronic uncontrolled asthma, and pre-eclampsia. Authors of a meta-analysis of case-control studies of Cp biomarkers and chronic asthma in children and adults found C. pneumoniae-specific IgE was strongly associated with both asthma and asthma severity. The population attributable risk for C. pneumoniae-specific IgE was 47% (95% CI 39%-55%).
Chlamydia pneumonia is a CAP caused by C. pneumoniae, an obligate intracellular bacteria.
C. pneumoniae infection is probably widespread (with over 50% of children testing positive for prior exposure), but symptoms are either mild or not present.
Immunity to infection does not last long, making recurrent or persistent infection possible.

Observational studies have suggested a link between C. pneumoniae infection and atherosclerotic heart disease. However, a meta-analysis of 11 RCTs including 19,217 patients demonstrated that treatment of patients who had coronary artery disease (CAD) with antichlamydial antibiotics did not improve secondary prevention of heart disease or mortality. A
No single clinical or radiographic finding or constellation of findings accurately differentiates CAP caused by C. pneumoniae from any other cause. C

No single accurate, rapid, widely available, and validated diagnostic test exists for identification of C. pneumoniae. C Serology and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) are used for diagnosis in research studies.
Sputum or nasopharyngeal swab culture is considered the gold standard of diagnosis but is not recommended for routine use in patients with CAP. C Culture is relatively insensitive for C. pneumoniae.

Differential.Differential_Name: Typical pneumonia (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis)

Differential.Differential_Features: High-risk populations, history of choking or aspiration

Differential.Differential_Name: Zoonotic pneumonia (Chlamydia psittaci, Coxiella burnetii, Francisella tularensis, Yersinia pestis)

Differential.Differential_Features: Exposure history, positive purified protein derivative

list.listitem: Symptoms of Chlamydia pneumonia are the same as for CAP of any cause, including cough, fever, and dyspnea. Physical examination findings could include abnormal breath sounds (e.g., crackles), tachypnea, and signs of hypoxemia (e.g., cyanosis).
Patients with Chlamydia pneumonia tend to have symptoms that develop more gradually and have less cough than typical pathogens.
However, no individual finding or constellation of signs and symptoms can accurately differentiate pneumonia caused by C. pneumoniae from any other cause of CAP.
CXR cannot differentiate CAP caused by C. pneumoniae from other pathogens, but it is used as a prognostic factor.
Sputum or nasopharyngeal swab culture is considered the reference standard, but it is difficult and slow, has a variable yield, and has limited availability.

The Infectious Disease Society of America (IDSA) CAP treatment guideline (2019) recommends against obtaining sputum gram stains and sputum or blood cultures routinely in adults with CAP. Pretreatment gram stain and culture from respiratory secretions and blood cultures are recommended for those with severe CAP, those being empirically treated for or previously infected with methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus or Pseudomonas aeruginosa, or those hospitalized and receiving antibiotics within the past 90 days. For additional testing recommendations for patients at higher risk for Legionella spp. or influenza, see the IDSA guideline.
Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) with enzyme immunoassay is promising as a rapid diagnostic test but is not standardized or validated; PCR and IgM serology appear to be more sensitive than culture.
Modifications made with PCR assays including multiplex TaqMan real-time PCR and touchdown enzyme time-release PCR show promise in improving diagnostic accuracy for Chlamydia spp.

In a study of 75 children in India with lower respiratory tract infection, C. pneumoniae infection was positive in 11 (14.6%) children by serology and nested PCR. Using PCR as the standard, serology had a 77.8% sensitivity, 92.4% specificity, 58.3% positive predictive value and 96.8% negative predictive value
Monoclonal antibodies for use in immunofluorescence and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays are promising screening tools under development for chlamydia pneumonia.

The Center for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) considers a single IgM titer of 1:16 or higher or a 4-fold increase in IgG titer by microimmunofluorescence as the only acceptable serologic test for C. pneumoniae, yet titers still suffer from poor specificity (according to the CDC) and sensitivity (25% compared with culture). Acute and convalescent IgG titers are more sensitive than a single time-point titer but do not offer rapid diagnosis.
Follow diagnostic guidelines (history, physical examination, CXR, and other selected studies) for CAP.
Specific tests for chlamydia (e.g., PCR or antibody titers) are not widely available or clinically useful.
Refer to chapter on Pneumonia (community acquired pneumonia) for more on management.
Specific coverage of atypical pathogens such as C. pneumoniae in outpatients and hospitalized patients with undifferentiated CAP does not reduce mortality.B
Choice of antibiotics for undifferentiated CAP should be dictated by local microbial and resistance patterns. C
Empiric treatment for CAP in outpatients with no comorbidities is monotherapy with amoxicillin, doxycycline, or a macrolide (if local pneumococcal resistance is <25%).
Treatment of CAP for culture or serologically-proven C. pneumoniae includes doxycycline or a macrolide as first-line therapy, or a fluoroquinolone as an alternative. C

Because of the inability to differentiate specific pathogens causing pneumonia at the time of diagnosis, initial therapy of CAP should be empiric and dictated by the evidence for treatment of CAP as a whole.

IDSA recommends empiric treatment for CAP in outpatients with no comorbidities as monotherapy with amoxicillin, doxycycline, or a macrolide (if local pneumococcal resistance is <25%). For inpatients with non-severe pneumonia, they recommend a beta-lactam plus macrolide or a respiratory fluroquinalone and for severe pneumonia a beta-lactam plus macrolide or a beta-lactam plus respiratory fluroquinalone. For additional recommendations, see the chapter on pneumonia, community acquired.

A network meta-analysis of 24 randomized trials compared initial oral antibiotics for CAP. While trends suggested better outcomes with empiric fluoroquinolones, no conclusive evidence favored one antibiotic over another.

No significant difference in clinical failure rates were observed when treating CAP with either macrolides or fluoroquinolones based on a meta-analysis of 5 RCTs. For CAP associated with any atypical bacteria, the RR was 1.57 (95% CI 0.73-3.38, I2 0%) and for CAP associated with C. pneumoniae the RR was 2.12 (95% CI 0.63 to 7.14, I2 0%).

Authors of two meta-analyses of 18 RCTs with 6749 outpatients and 24 RCTs with 5015 inpatients found no benefit for empiric atypical pathogen coverage compared with beta-lactam therapy alone for both outpatients and hospitalized patients with CAP. No RCTs comparing beta-lactam therapy with beta-lactam plus atypical coverage are available at this time.
If C. pneumoniae is identified as the causative pathogen, doxycycline or a macrolide are first-line agents. Fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin, ciprofloxacin, moxifloxacin, ofloxacin) are alternatives.

Mixed infection is common and must be considered in treatment failures. In one case series of 49 mechanically-ventilated patients with severe CAP, viruses were involved in almost half (5 probably pure viral infections and 19 mixed bacterial-viral).

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 19 RCTs and 2 additional trials of CAP management with short-course treatment, defined as ≤6 days, vs. treatment for ≥7 days found comparable cure rates regardless of setting or pneumonia severity, similar relapse rates, and lower risk of serious adverse events (1,923 patients, RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.55-0.97) and lower mortality (2,802 patients, RR 0.52, 95% CI 0.33-0.82).
Consider hospitalization if signs and symptoms (e.g., hypoxemia, tachypnea) or patient demographics (age, comorbidities) would place the patient at elevated risk of morbidity and mortality.
Clinical decision rules such as the CURB-65 and the Pneumonia Severity Index exist for assessing severity of illness.
Recurrent or chronic infection is possible. C
Consider C. pneumoniae as a possible etiology in pneumonia outbreaks in nursing home populations. B
Patients with both bacterial and viral infection have more serious CAP, as measured by pneumonia severity index, than those with a bacterial pathogen alone (OR 4.98; 95% CI 2.09-11.89).
C. pneumoniae is more likely than M. pneumoniae in an older population.
